articles.title: Politics of agitation
articles.content: SEPTEMBER emerged as a politically charged month. The PTI and Jamaat-i-Islami announced theirplansfor long marches on Islamabad. The simultaneous mobilisation by the two parties had raised concerns about potentially prolonged street protests and disruptions in the capital. However, both partiespostponedtheir marches (although the PTI has indicated it would begin its protest over the weekend), which temporarily eased the immediate concern of large-scale agitation. But, despite the postponements, the episode has once again highlighted the recurring pattern of opposition parties resorting to street agitation. It has raised several questions regarding the rationale of this politics of agitation. Why do some political parties in Pakistan consistently resort to street agitation, road blockades, and prolonged sit-ins, while others continue to place their faith in parliamentary procedures and institutional mechanisms? What does this divergence reveal about the country’s political culture? These questions lie at the heart of understanding the recurring cycle of protests that has come to define much of Pakistan’s contemporary politics. In Pakistan’s political culture, agitation has recently served as a potent instrument for opposition parties to convert street power into tangible political gains through the ballot box. By orchestrating prolonged protests and sit-ins, parties have succeeded in mobilising their grassroots workers, reinvigorating cadre loyalty, and projecting an image of resistance against the status quo. Excessive media coverage provides publicity that often elevates relatively smaller actors to the level of national relevance, while the narrative of standing up for the ‘common man’ against an unresponsive system helps cultivate a saviour-like persona. This dynamic was most visibly demonstrated by the PTI, whose 2014 Islamabad dharna and 2016 ‘lockdown’ agitation not only kept the party in the headlines for months but also laid the organisational and perceptual groundwork for its dramatic electoral expansion in 2018. Through this strategy, the PTI secured phenomenal electoral gains, from a modest 34 National Assembly seats in 2013 to 120 seats in 2018. Since 2012, the state’s response to political agitation has undergone a noticeable evolution. Similar patterns are evident at the regional levels. The TLP registered itself as a political party in 2016 and after its long march on Islamabad in November 2017, it remarkably secured 2.2 million votes in the 2018 elections. Maulana Hidayatur Rehman’s sustained agitation in Gwadar transformed him from a marginal local political figure into a formidable voice of Gwadar, while Hafiz Naeemur Rehman’s high-visibility protests in Karachi have allowed the Jamaat-i-Islami to reclaim political space in urban Sindh. It is precisely this proven formula of converting agitation into both visibility and voter sympathy that appears to have encouraged the current Jamaat chief to attempt replicating the strategy on a national scale. At its core, however, the recurring resort to agitation also reflects a deep lack of trust in the government, legitimacy of the electoral system, and the taxation system, compounded by the widespread perception of corruption. When citizens believe that taxes are routinely misappropriated rather than spent on public welfare, protests become the default language of political expression, as institutional channels are viewed as ineffective or compromised. However, this strategy of political agitation also carries significant socioeconomic costs. Prolonged protests and road blockades not only disrupt daily economic activities, they also impose heavy financial burdens on businesses, trade, and ordinary citizens. The PTI’s 2014 Islamabad sit-ins, which stretched for 126 days, and the subsequent waves of agitation in later years, created extended periods of uncertainty, including around 152 days of political and economic instability within a span of two years. As per a recent statement by the finance minister, every single day of protest may inflict aneconomic lossof around Rs120 billion on Pakistan’s economy. When this figure is applied to the 152 days of protests witnessed over the past decade, the cumulative financial damage is staggering and exposes the severe economic cost of sustained political agitation. These disruptions led to substantial losses in the trade, transport, and retail sectors, while simultaneously damaging market sentiment and eroding investor confidence, as prolonged street unrest signals political instability and policy unpredictability. Since 2012, the state’s response to political agitation has undergone a noticeable evolution. In the earlier phase, the government largely avoided direct confrontation. Instead, it opted for dialogue and negotiation. Federal ministers were frequently nominated by the prime minister of the time to engage with protest leaders, as seen during Tahirul Qadri’s 2012-13 sit-ins in Islamabad, the PTI’s prolonged 2014 dharna, and the TLP’s 2017 long march. These episodes reflected the government’s preference for political management over force. From 2012 to 2017, the state apparatus largely attempted to defuse tensions through concessions or mediated settlements rather than immediate crackdowns. Over time, however, this approach has shifted towards greater repression. Successive governments have increasingly relied on heavy-handed tactics, including the use of force, communication blackout, mass arrests, and restrictions on movement to disperse protests. While this strategy has, to some extent, discouraged repeated large-scale national-level agitations by raising the cost of mobilisation, it has simultaneously deepened public resentment towards state institutions. The perception of an increasingly authoritarian response has further eroded public trust in the system, and reinforced the very sense of institutional alienation that often fuels street protests in the first place. Although both the Jamaat and PTI postponed their long marches to Islamabad, the underlying tension between the opposition’s inclination towards street agitation and the government’s readiness to suppress such mobilisations remains. This recurring pattern continues to raise important questions: Can Pakistan continue to afford the repeated economic and institutional costs of agitation and repression? Or will the state and political actors eventually recognise the need to strengthen formal institutions such as the judiciary, parliament, and the standing committees of the National Assembly and Senate so that grievances can be resolved through dialogue and established democratic mechanisms rather than through the streets? The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.
articles.author: Khurram Abbas

articles.title: ‘China model’ fallacies
articles.content: ECONOMIC discourse in this country, especially with folks in governance circles, can throw up some very interesting — as well as disturbing — insights. A recent conversation brought up the interesting case of a preference for the ‘China model’. What is their conception of this model? Briefly, the belief is in an all-powerful centre that forces its economic commands through long-term plans across the entire country, whips up economic growth through major government interventions, and leaves a limited role for the lower tiers (local) of governance. It is worth contemplating whether these views align with ground realities. A good place to start is the recent paper by Fengming Lu and Xiao Ma, ‘The rise of China’s electric vehicle industry’, which helps demolish several myths. Champion EV firms like BYD and NIO are all private firms that did not get a single penny in state grants, which, instead, went to SOEs for EV research. Even more astonishing, these firms rose in cities the state apparatus did not identify for EV cluster development. How, then, did these firms accomplish this feat? The short answer: mayors of the cities that were left out teamed up with entrepreneurs, helping them usher in the latest achievement of China’s stellar development story. Notice that city mayors have the authority to act as they please within their locality. In this case, their initiative and actions undermined the SOEs. Yet, the central government never intervened to prevent it, thus demolishing the myth of an all-powerful centre that micromanages everything and does not tolerate local authority. The Chinese state mainly acts as a facilitator for development in any way it can. In Pakistan, it’s the opposite. China has a highly competitive and well-established local tier system. Passage to the higher echelons of the central party is possible only through performance at this level. Unlike in Pakistan, there is no chance of attaining a prominent party position merely by being a scion or progeny of a party head. (Interested readers can look up President Xi Jinping’s road to the presidency.) Second, it demonstrates that the state is willing to tolerate ‘creative destruction’, a term coined by economist Joseph Schumpeter, to describe how competition and creativity can render some businesses useless. This is classic capitalism, not socialism or communism. In the race for EVs, private competitors left state-run SOEs far behind, but the centre never intervened to prevent their slide. In fact, competition is so intense that it has led to price wars, with some firms expected to fail (one county reportedly lost 6.6 billion yuan on a carmaker it supported). Similar misconceptions exist around its long-term plans. These actually contain insights of tremendous depth, coming from top-tier experts. Plans are contemplated and debated at length rather than rushed through. The economic debates preceding the 14th party congress offer an apt illustration. In the wake of the Soviet Union’s collapse, between October and December 1991 (known as ‘eleven half-days’), the debate centred on why the USSR’s economy collapsed and what could be done to prevent the same from happening to China. The end result was the adoption of the famous ‘modern enterprise system’, approved by the party in November 1993, which enunciated “clear property rights, clearly defined rights and responsibilities, separation of government and enterprise, and scientific management”, that would prove to be a critical moment in China’s march to prosperity. The gist is that prevailing conceptions of China as a centrally administered economy with a benevolent dictator at the helm directing its stellar rise are misplaced. In fact, it is arguably the most decentralised governance system in the world, with more than 80 per cent of public expenditure at the local level, and mayors who enjoy independence in their fiscal and administrative decision-making. The centre is still very powerful, but not in a manner that we understand. It has some red lines that it enforces. The rich, for example, are not allowed to attain influence to an extent that they are in a position to manipulate the state apparatus by tailoring it in their favour to the detriment of the country and its people. This explains, for example, why Communist Party members are banned from holding golf club memberships. The underlying philosophy is simple: facilitate capital creation and growth, but prevent it from working against the public good and the country. The state mainly acts as a facilitator for development in any way it can. In Pakistan, it’s the complete opposite. Big capital dictates and manipulates policies, whether through tax exemptions or trillions doled out in public-sector contracts. The sugar mafia is a pertinent example, whose powerful members, sitting in the legislature, sway policies and regulations in their favour. (Note: the above should not be taken as advocacy for anti-capital formation policies. Instead, it should be viewed in terms of regulating capital’s negative spillovers.) And lest we forget, the corrupt in China are handed the death penalty. Try naming a few cases in Pakistan where a similar predicament befell the corrupt. In essence, China’s remarkable transformation to where it stands today constitutes a long, arduous, and messy process that began with Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 reforms, with the above merely offering a glimpse of that long journey. Why then clamour for this ‘model’ that no one in our power halls would be willing to implement? After all, that would be hara-kiri for a corrupt, compromised elite which thrives on central control and illegally accrued rents via this system. Well, more than four years into the current experiment, the economy is still struggling to get out of the stagflationary rut in which it has been stuck since 2022; the average GDP growth has barely surpassed population growth, and all the ‘game changers’ (SIFC, $6 trillion mineral wealth, corporate farming, crypto, and geopolitical rents) have fizzled out. Expectedly, in comes yet another game changer — the ‘China model’. I cannot speak for others, but if it were up to me, I’d start implementing this model tomorrow. I assume, though, that once the enthusiastic folks in power circles come to grips with what it really implies, they’ll discard it immediately. The writer is an economist. His current research focuses on long-term analyses of the various issues plaguing Pakistan’s economy, economic reforms and the history of economic thought.
articles.author: Shahid Mehmood

articles.title: Finding balance
articles.content: PARENTING is one of the hardest jobs in the world. When we become parents, we are suddenly responsible for helping shape another human being — how they see themselves, how they treat others, and eventually how they face the world. Yet most of us begin this enormous responsibility with no training at all. There is no single formula for good parenting. Every child is different. Even newborn babies have different temperaments: some are calm, while others are difficult to settle. Genetics plays a role, as does the environment in which a child grows. Parents and family have an enormous influence, but as children grow, teachers, friends, school, social media, and life experiences increasingly shape who they become. It would be unfair to blame parents alone when a teenager develops mental health or behavioural problems, becomes violent, uses drugs or takes other dangerous paths. Nevertheless, positive parenting can have a powerful influence. Research on parenting styles broadly describes four approaches: authoritative, authoritarian, permissive and neglectful. Authoritative parenting is characterised by warmth, support and structure while fostering autonomy. These parents give teenagers enough independence to make decisions with reasonable rules and boundaries. Authoritarian parents tend to control their children, enforce strict rules and rely more on punishment than problem-solving. Permissive parents are loving and responsive but place few demands on their children, with few boundaries or clear expectations. Neglectful parents are emotionally distant and provide little supervision, guidance, or support. Adolescence (10 to 19 years) is a time of major physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development. For some, it is a roller-coaster ride; for others, it is a relatively balanced experience. Adolescents begin to identify themselves as individuals separate from their parents. They form their own self-image, seek privacy and become increasingly influenced by their peers. At the same time, the parts of the brain involved in judgement, impulse control and understanding long-term consequences are still developing. This is where the challenge of parenting a teenager is particularly evident. They may act like adults but are not adults yet. Supervision is necessary, though it should allow them to feel liberated rather than suffocated. They may not like their parents’ interference but still need their physical and emotional support. Making rules, providing structure and routine, and setting boundaries are all important. Involving teenagers when making rules and allowing them to voice their concerns helps build their self-confidence. If they break rules, discussions should follow. Simply lecturing them and pointing out their mistake won’t produce positive results. Listening to them does not mean agreeing with everything they say or giving up parental authority. It tells them that their thoughts and feelings matter and makes it more likely that they will approach their parents if they face a serious problem. Crucially, parents should know their teenagers’ friends, where they are going and what they are doing, including in the online world, while also giving their offspring more freedom as they demonstrate increasing responsibility. Clothes, hairstyles, music and other harmless choices are often part of developing an identity and fitting in with friends. Avoiding unnecessary confrontation over these matters may make it easier to be firm when parental intervention really matters, such as with drugs, violence, safety or other risky behaviour. We cannot always protect our children from making mistakes or wrong decisions. But rather than covering up their mistakes or immediately rescuing them from the consequences, it is important that they are helped in understanding the difference between right and wrong so that they can make better choices in the future. Finally, parents instil values most effectively by being role models. Practising what is important to us is often more powerful than repeatedly telling our children what they should do. We cannot teach respect by humiliating them, honesty by being dishonest ourselves, or self-control by losing our temper. Teenagers may appear rebellious and sometimes reject what we teach them, but what they observe at home stays with them long after adolescence is over. Parenting a teenager is therefore a balancing act. They need independence but also boundaries, privacy but also supervision, freedom but also responsibility. Perhaps parents’ job during these years is not to make every decision for them, but gradually to teach them how to make good decisions for themselves. The goal of parenting is not simply to raise an obedient teenager, but to raise a responsible, compassionate and independent adult.
articles.author: Kishwar Enam

articles.title: Afghan irredentism
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S relations with Afghanistan have remained hostage to Afghan irredentism, which is a consequence of deep-seated historical animosities. The antipathy towards Pakistan was engendered through a false sense of entitlement about areas of Pakistan that in the past had once supposedly been part of Afghanistan. Generations in Afghanistan have been reared on a distorted version of history that regards the Pak-Afghan border as a historical injustice. Little do these irredentists know that going by that logic Afghanistan has remained part of the Maurya and Mughal empires, while Sikhs, under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, had advanced up to Peshawar in 1834. Subsequently, the British and Afghans kept sparring over territories across British India and the Afghan frontier, resulting in three Anglo-Afghan wars. The frontier between British India and Afghanistan was formalised in 1893 through the Durand Line Agreement between Emir Abdur Rahman of Afghanistan and Sir Henry Mortimer Durand, foreign secretary of British India. In fact, it was Emir Abdur Rahman who wanted to formalise Afghanistan’s borders both with Russia and British India. Abdur Rahman requested the British Indian government to delineate the border between the two states. He specifically requested Mortimer Durand to lead the mission. Following the agreement, joint commissions demarcated the border over several years and thereafter, several treaties were concluded. Each reaffirmed both parties’ commitments to respecting the boundary. Afghan irredentism has kept emerging with regularity. During the course of demarcation, Afghanistan gained territory not only from British India but also from Russia and Iran. As a legatee state of British India, Pakistan inherited the border agreement as per the customary international law principle of uti possidetis juris (new states inherit pre-existing borders). However, Afghanistan’s representative cast the sole dissenting vote against Pakistan’s inclusion in the UN. Though that negative vote was removed after a few weeks, the bad blood of Afghan irredentism continued to plague bilateral ties. A Loya Jirga declared all previous agreements regarding the international boundary invalid in July 1949, followed by border skirmishes and diplomatic stand-offs. Afghan forces entered Pakistani territory and were repelled after six days. Afghanistan kept providing political and financial support to Pakhtunistan-oriented elements in the 1950s while Afghan prime minister Mohammad Daoud condemned Pakistan’s One Unit arrangement, promising Afghan government support to Pakhtuns in Pakistan. Afghan mobs violated Pakistan’s diplomatic missions at Kabul, Jalalabad and Kandahar. Afghan troops in disguise, along with anti-Pakistan tribesmen, entered Bajaur in September 1960 under the direction of prime minister Daoud. Local tribesmen and Frontier Corps scouts initially resisted their advance while regular Pakistani forces, including air force and artillery, beat back Afghan troops, souring relations till 1963. After the deposition of King Zahir Shah by Daoud in 1973, Afghan intervention in Pakistan became more brazen. Afghanistan openly supported pro-Pakhtunistan elements. Afghanistan under Sardar Daoud also remained a veritable support base for the Baloch insurgency. Despite maximum support to Afghans in their freedom struggle during the Soviet invasion (1979-89), Afghan irredentism kept emerging with metronomic regularity, irrespective of the regime in power. From 1996 to 2001, Taliban-controlled Afghanistan kept harbouring terrorist organisations including Al Qaeda, ETIM, and IMU. These groups influenced Pakistan’s ex-Fata region as well. The armed groups based in Afghan territory kept conducting cross-border attacks against Pakistan from 2002 to 2006, encouraging the rise of terrorist entities like TTP. When Pakistan finally started fencing its border in 2017, Afghan troops targeted Pakistani forces at Torkham, repeating similar actions at Parachinar, Chaman, Bajaur and Chitral. Pakistan had welcomed the Taliban regime after the 2021 US withdrawal in good neighbourly spirit, offering humanitarian and economic support at a time when most of the world was treating it as a pariah regime. The Taliban regime in turn gave impetus to anti-Pakistan terrorists like the TTP holed up in Afghanistan. In 2021, terrorist incidents saw a 42 per cent rise, owing to the Afghan Taliban’s takeover of Kabul and the subsequent release of hardened militants from various Afghan jails. From 128 terrorist incidents in 2021 to over 1,200 in 2025, there has been a steady rise in Taliban-regime enabled terrorist violence in Pakistan. Despite continued positive engagement by Pakistan, the Taliban regime has displayed obduracy and non-cooperation on the counterterrorism front by using terrorism as a low-cost option for leverage.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: Risks ahead
articles.content: ON Thursday, a day after the PTI leadership expressed its resolve to go ahead with its planned protest march this weekend, the question of ‘what now?’ continued to hang heavy in the air. Over the course of the day, the government kept signalling it was contemplating governor’s rule or imposing emergency in KP, with ameetingbetween the prime minister and president announced in this regard. Meanwhile, senior opposition leaders set strict terms for possible talks with the government, which they announced at a press conference after a multiparty meeting. It also appeared that the PTI had prepared itself mentally for extreme consequences, with its interim chairman and a senior leader directly addressing the government on the possibility of special administrative measures being imposed in KP, warning that such an action would not resolve issues and only benefit “non-democratic powers”. The prime minister sought counsel from his allies in the PPP, with a meeting between him and the president on Thursday evening, concluding with a decision to talk to the opposition on Friday. The prime minister was earlier slated to take the president into confidence regarding the political and security climate, including the possibility of emergency or governor’s rule in KP. It may be recalled that the PPP had also been invited to the opposition multiparty moot, but it did not attend. After the multiparty meeting, the opposition leaders in the National Assembly and Senate sounded defiant, even angry. NA opposition leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai, who had just days ago been invited by the prime minister for talks, ruled out meeting the latter in the Prime Minister’s Office or PM House in an uncharacteristically terse statement to the media, even calling the chief executive “illegitimate”. The Senate opposition leader, Raja Nasir Abbas, spoke in a similar vein, saying, “We are fully prepared to hold dialogue and correct the situation, but this will be without any conditions. If anyone thinks that they will hold a dagger to our necks, then such a thing will never be accepted.” Only the latter is expected to join the Friday talks. It seems that a confrontation could still be avoided if the jailed PTI founder is granted some time in hospital and visits from his lawyers and family. Both those things had already beenorderedby the Supreme Court in August. To think that the government would rather push out an elected government than grant a single prisoner some facilities does not square up rationally. As the side holding the cards, it bears greater responsibility. Likewise, the PTI should also weigh its options judiciously, instead of reaching directly for another direct confrontation. It can only be hoped that sense prevails between now and Sunday. The country cannot afford more upheaval.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Exit from Iraq
articles.content: AMERICAN and British troops have once again shipped out of Iraq. On Wednesday, the foreign forces left the Arab country as per an agreement with the Iraqi government in 2024 that called for wrapping up their decade-old mission against the self-styled Islamic State group. While this deployment was requested by the Iraqis, the Americans and their allies had earlier arrived uninvited, invading Iraq in 2003 to topple its strongman Saddam Hussein. That misadventure had left Iraq in ruins, torn apart by sectarian civil war and a terrorist onslaught by IS. On Wednesday, there was great joy on the streets of Baghdad, indicating that many Iraqis were happy to see the foreign forces go home. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi termed it “a new phase” and declared that Oct 1 would be observed as ‘Sovereignty Day’ every year. Long after IS had been mostly neutralised, the US military presence in Iraq had actually become a liability, with American bases attacked by both Iran and the pro-Tehran Hashd as-Shaabi militias. US President Donald Trump welcomed the latest withdrawal as a “victory”. However, though justifying the need to bring his troops home from Iraq, Mr Trump has gotten stuck in a quagmire because of his war with Iran. The fact is that American military bases in the Middle East offer only an illusion of security. In reality, they have been a source of instability. Not only have these facilities been used to destabilise and occupy regional states — Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, etc — they also put targets on the countries that host them. The fantasy of the American security umbrella was very quickly shattered for the Gulf states when Iranian missiles targeted them, as Tehran claimed that the attacks against it were launched from these US bases. Following the example of its departure from Iraq, the US must further reduce its military footprint in the Middle East. It is by no means a global policeman, and its military forays have only resulted in chaos in the region. Instead, the people of the region — the Arabs, Iranians, Turks, and other nations — should be able to work out a mutual security structure based on non-aggression. The age of empire and Cold War calculations is over. Sovereign states of the Middle East can decide their fate for themselves, and do not need powerful external patrons to ‘protect’ them.
articles.author: Editorial
